1. Coherence lens  
   • Soundness: Mostly. It correctly identifies that “dispersed knowledge” is used consistently across the two sub-domains.  
   • Quibble: In this calibration entry both “Hayek – dispersed knowledge” and “Markets – price signals” sit within economics, so there’s actually no real cross-domain equivocation to catch. The lens treats them as distinct domains when they’re really two facets of the same field. The logic holds internally, but it’s certifying coherence where the framing itself already guaranteed it.  

2. Testability lens  
   • Unsound. Pointing to Hayek’s 1945 essay as “named theorem or historical evidence” conflates citation with falsifiability. “The Use of Knowledge in Society” lays out an argument but does not propose a clear, operationalizable hypothesis with predicted empirical patterns. A proper testability check would ask: “Does the claim yield specific, measurable variables and proposed experiments or data-patterns that could refute it?” Simply naming an essay is not sufficient.  

3. Triviality lens  
   • Unsound. Stripping the claim to “distributed information + signaling” over-generalizes away the very mechanism Hayek isolated: that competitive price formation simultaneously aggregates dispersed local knowledge and incentivizes resource reallocation without central computation. That is not a generic property of complex systems but a specific economic insight. The lens’s abstraction killed the nuance and wrongly labeled a Nobel-winning insight as “trivial.”  

4. Final verdict and scoring  
   • The 2-of-3 survival rule mechanically promotes the claim, but because the Testability and Triviality lenses misfire, the promotion is misleading. This Nobel-ground-truth should have passed Coherence and failed Triviality (declared non-trivial), while Testability should have been marked “UNDETERMINED” or “POORLY SPECIFIED” rather than a pass.  
   • Awarding 42 points as “ADJACENT_ACTIVE” overstates novelty (the pipeline itself verified this was long-settled theory) and misallocates credit given the lens errors.  

5. Sharpened lens definitions  
   • Coherence: Verify that the bisociated domains employ the key terms in genuinely distinct contexts and check for true analogical mapping rather than re-labeling the same discipline.  
   • Testability: Demand a clear statement of variables, mechanisms, and empirical or experimental criteria by which the claim could be falsified or supported. Citation alone is not a test.  
   • Triviality: Assess whether the mechanism in question is a non-obvious, field-specific explanatory advance rather than a restatement of a generic complex-systems pattern.

1. Coherence lens  
   • Lens claim: “Both domains utilize ‘frame-dependence’ in the same formal sense, so the bisociation is coherent.”  
   • What fails:  
     – In electromagnetism prior to Einstein, Maxwell’s equations are not usually described as “frame-dependent” at all but rather as predicting an invariant speed c (i.e. frame-invariance of c). By contrast, special relativity introduces genuine frame-dependence of time and length. Equating these two distinct uses of “frame-dependence” glosses over the real difference between (a) a law that happens to single out a universal constant c and (b) a kinematic framework that makes space and time themselves relative.  
     – A true coherence check would align the symmetry groups or transformation laws (Galilean vs. Lorentz) and ask: does the hypothesis correctly map Maxwell’s Lorentz-symmetry requirement onto relativity’s postulates? Merely noting both talk about “frames” is too shallow.  

2. Testability lens  
   • Lens claim: “Referencing Einstein’s 1905 paper makes the claim testable.”  
   • What fails:  
     – Testability in a scientific sense means the hypothesis yields concrete, empirical predictions that could in principle be falsified (e.g. time dilation, length contraction, null result of Michelson–Morley). Citing a historical document is about verifiability of provenance, not empirical testability of the scientific content.  
     – A proper testability check would require the claim to specify at least one measurable effect unique to the Maxwell-to-relativity inference (for example, the exact form of Lorentz transformations needed to keep Maxwell’s equations invariant), and then point to experimental confirmation of that effect.  
   
3. Triviality lens  
   • Lens claim: “Mapping one theoretical framework’s inconsistency onto another and fixing it is a generic pattern in complex systems, so the claim is trivial.”  
   • What fails:  
     – The bisociation here is highly non-generic: before Einstein there was no principled way to reconcile a universal wave speed with Galilean relativity. The specific mathematical structure (Lorentz invariance) emerged uniquely from taking Maxwell seriously. You cannot substitute “complex system A” and “framework B” arbitrarily and get the same story.  
     – A real triviality check would ask: is this mapping an obvious corollary of definitions, or did it require the invention of a new transformation group (Lorentz group)? Here it is the latter.  

4. Final verdict and scoring  
   • Survives 2/3 refutations: that outcome is correct for a true historical claim.  
   • But the triviality lens’s false positive and the testability lens’s mis-application signal miscalibration. The ensemble rule masked these individual failures.  
   • The “ADJACENT_ACTIVE” verification verdict also undersells the case: this is not merely “adjacent” evidence but well-documented historical fact that Maxwell’s constant c drove the formulation of special relativity. A stronger “SUPPORTED” or “CONFIRMED” category would be more appropriate.  
   • The flat 42-point award for a calibration benchmark may inflate confidence in the mis-firing lenses; calibration cases should ideally push the score to maximum only when all lenses apply their criteria correctly.  

5. Sharper lens definitions  
   – Coherence should test for formal isomorphism of transformation laws (e.g. mapping the Lorentz invariance of the electromagnetic tensor onto relativity’s postulates), not loose term-matching.  
   – Testability should require at least one explicit, falsifiable prediction derived from the bisociation (e.g. quantitative time-dilation formula, null Michelson–Morley result) and documented experimental confirmation.  
   – Triviality should assess whether the cross-domain mapping yields a non-obvious explanatory leap—e.g. the invention of the Lorentz group—versus a routine parameter adjustment. If the mapping merely restates a definitional corollary, it’s trivial; if it demands new structure, it isn’t.

1. Lens-by-lens critique

Coherence — SURVIVES  
• What it did well: It spotted that both evolutionary biology and non-cooperative game theory invoke “Nash equilibrium” (in the former as the core of an ESS).  
• What it missed: It treats ESS and Nash equilibrium as wholly interchangeable, glossing over the fact that ESS is a strict refinement of the symmetric Nash equilibrium concept (every ESS is a Nash equilibrium, but not vice versa). A true coherence check should demand that the hypothesis either acknowledge that extra “stability‐against‐invasion” condition or justify collapsing the two definitions entirely.

Testability — SURVIVES (but unsound)  
• Where it goes wrong: It equates “there exists a precise theorem in the literature” with “the claim is empirically or computationally falsifiable.” Under its rubric, pointing to Maynard-Smith & Price’s proof counts as “testability,” whereas the original intention of the lens is to ensure a hypothesis yields a clear, operational experiment or simulation that could conceivably disprove it in the real world. Conflating “theorem checkability” with “falsifiability” is a design flaw.

Triviality — SURVIVES  
• What it did well: It recognized that this isn’t a hand-wavy “X often happens” statement but a specific mapping.  
• What it missed: By its own standard of weeding out “mere restatement of definitions,” it should have at least flagged that the hypothesis is literally the definition of an ESS (i.e. “a strategy that resists invasion is, by definition, a symmetric Nash equilibrium with stability conditions”). As phrased, the claim adds no insight beyond the textbook definition.

2. Verdict and scoring

• Collision verdict (“not novel”) is correct.  
• Promotion on 3/3 survival is consistent with the existing promotion rule—but awarding 25 public leaderboard points to a hand-authored calibration benchmark is miscalibrated. Calibration cases should not inflate the engine’s competitive score; they ought to be tracked separately or marked “non-competitive.”

3. Sharpened lens definitions

Coherence (revised):  
“Check that each concept in Domain A really maps to its counterpart in Domain B, including all extra constraints or refinements. If one is a strict refinement of the other, the hypothesis must explicitly address or justify that refinement rather than treating the two as identical.”

Testability (revised):  
“Require the hypothesis to spell out an empirical or computational protocol—an experiment or simulation with clear inputs, measurable outputs, and a predetermined rejection threshold—so that it could, in principle, be falsified in practice, not merely proven in theory.”

Triviality (revised):  
“Flag as trivial any hypothesis that merely restates a domain definition or a one-to-one renaming of an existing concept. To survive, a claim must contribute an independent linkage or insight beyond embedded definitions.”

1. Lens-by-lens soundness  
  – Coherence (SURVIVES)  
    *Soundness check:* The lens correctly asks whether “independence axiom” means the same formal thing in both psychology and economics, and finds no equivocation. That is exactly the right test here, and its reasoning holds.  
  – Testability (SURVIVES)  
    *Soundness check:* The lens correctly identifies that the Allais paradox and the measurable Prospect-Theory value function provide crisp, reproducible tests of the claim. Its criteria and conclusion are solid.  
  – Triviality (REFUTED)  
    *Misstep:* The lens collapses “a structured, domain-specific violation of a single axiom via loss aversion” into “any complex system predictably deviates from its model,” and then bangs on “that applies broadly, so it’s trivial.” That over-generalization is unsound. Prospect Theory’s specific mechanism (steeper loss curve) and its empirical signature (Allais paradox patterns) are non-generic and non-vacuous. The triviality lens here commits a false negative by treating a precise behavioral regularity as if it were a banal meta-claim about all models.

2. Final verdict and scoring  
  – Verdict (“SURVIVES” on 2-of-3) is defensible. A gold-standard, Nobel-confirmed result should indeed survive.  
  – The triviality lens failure didn’t veto the claim, so the system’s net outcome is correct.  
  – Awarding 17 points for a verified claim that survives refutation aligns with the pipeline’s rubric (verify + survive ≈ mid-high score). No obvious miscalibration in the point total.

3. Suggested sharper lens formulations  
  – Coherence should remain a check for genuine shared terminology and structural mapping, but could also verify that domain-specific causal stories don’t secretly “means-different-things” equivocations.  
  – Testability should explicitly require (a) a clear experimental protocol and (b) parameter-measurement procedures, which it already does well here.  
  – Triviality should be tightened to ask: “If you remove all domain labels, does the remainder apply meaningfully to a wide class of systems, or does it collapse into a vacuous schema? If it only makes sense in the original domain, it is non-trivial.” Under that test, the claim about human loss aversion and the independence axiom would survive triviality.

Here’s a case‐by‐case critique of how the three lenses handled Planck’s real blackbody–quantization discovery:

1. Lens reasoning  

  • Coherence – SURVIVES  
    – Sound takeaway: both “domains” really do share the formal concept of energy exchange; mapping E = hf into thermodynamic balance equations is a coherent, non‐equivocal bisociation.  
    – Minor quibble: the write‐up treats “energy exchange” as if it needs no further unpacking; a more rigorous coherence test would demand a sketch of how Planck’s discrete oscillator model slots into the Maxwell–Boltzmann framework rather than appealing to a single shared term.  

  • Testability – SURVIVES  
    – Broadly defensible: Planck’s formula makes a definite prediction (the spectral radiance versus frequency curve) that can be—and has been—compared point-by-point with measured blackbody spectra.  
    – Overreach: citing the 1918 Nobel award as the ‘experiment’ confuses retrospective validation with the lens’s real purpose, which is to check whether the hypothesis itself lays out a clear, prospective means of falsification or measurement.  

  • Triviality – REFUTED  
    – Unsound. Planck’s law is famously non-trivial; it resolved a paradox classical theory could not even pose quantitatively. The lens’s test (“could this apply to any complex system?”) simply measures “genericness,” not triviality. A deep, novel law that unifies two fields will by definition have analogues elsewhere—it isn’t vacuous.  

2. Overall verdict & scoring  

  – VERDICT = SURVIVES is correct: this is a non-vacuous, coherent, testable claim.  
  – POINTS = 17 is miscalibrated. This was a _calibration benchmark_, not a machine‐generated insight that we want to reward. Either calibration entries should carry zero or separate “⟨Nobel‐gold⟩” points, or else they skew the leaderboard.  

3. Sharper lens definitions  

  • Coherence lens → “Isomorphic‐Mechanism Check”  
    Require an explicit sketch of how key operators or equations in domain A (continuous thermodynamic modes) map to those in domain B (quantized harmonic oscillators). Don’t just rely on shared terminology.  

  • Testability lens → “Prospective-Falsifiability Check”  
    Demand that the hypothesis itself specifies which measurements or calculations would confirm or disprove it—historical prestige or awards do not substitute for a clear experimental or computational protocol.  

  • Triviality lens → “Non-Vacuity (Novelty) Check”  
    Rather than asking “could this hold in many systems?” ask “does the claim assert more than a restatement of definitions or a well-known corollary of established theory?” In Planck’s case, it clearly does, so it should _pass_ non-vacuity.

Here’s a direct, lens-by-lens critique and suggestions for tightening:

1. Coherence Lens  
   – Stated reasoning: “Both domains use the same formal structure of feedback control; no equivocation.”  
   – What’s wrong: It never checks whether the lac operon really implements *negative* feedback as in control engineering. In fact, the lac system is a derepression switch—lactose removes inhibition, rather than the classic continuous error-driven negative feedback loop that stabilizes a variable around a setpoint. By glossing over that distinction it conflates two quite different control architectures.  
   – How to sharpen: Require the lens to verify that the *functional dynamics* (e.g. error calculation, continuous gain, setpoint correction) in the biological system map onto the same mathematical block diagram as in a prototypical negative-feedback controller, not just that both happen to use the word “feedback.”

2. Testability Lens  
   – Stated reasoning: “This is a well-documented historical experiment, so it’s testable and not vague.”  
   – What’s wrong: Testability should ask whether the *bisociation claim* (i.e. “the lac operon is formally identical to an engineering feedback controller”) makes new, concrete predictions you could still go measure—e.g. specific dynamic responses, gain margins, robustness properties—*beyond* simply “does lac repressor bind operator?” Pointing to the original papers that *discovered* the operon mechanism doesn’t satisfy that.  
   – How to sharpen: Insist that the hypothesis propose at least one fresh, measurable system property (time-constant, feedback gain, stability criterion) and show how to experimentally compare it to an engineered controller.

3. Triviality Lens  
   – Stated reasoning: “Lots of biological systems use feedback, so mapping lac→feedback is trivial.”  
   – What’s wrong: It collapses *all* feedback systems into a single trivial category. The lac operon mapping was *not* obvious at the time and required a precise identification of molecular players as controller, sensor, actuator. The lens never assesses the *novelty* or *specificity* of that mapping.  
   – How to sharpen: Require a measure of how *non-generic* the mapping is—e.g. count how many independent molecular-to-control-block correspondences must be invoked, or whether this particular feedback topology (inducible repression via ligand binding) appears in ≥N other contexts before being deemed “trivial.”

Verdict & Scoring  
– Because *all three* lenses misapply their own rubrics, the 2 / 3 “survives” outcome is a brittle fluke: we wanted a true claim to survive, but *for the wrong reasons*.  
– The 17-point score and “Survived Refutation” badge falsely suggest the pipeline’s refutation machinery is well-calibrated here, when in fact it never truly challenged the claim at the needed technical depth.

Overall, none of the three lenses held up under scrutiny. Each needs to be re-specified to test for (a) genuine structural equivalence (Coherence), (b) novel, falsifiable predictions (Testability), and (c) true cross-domain non-obviousness (Triviality).

1. Lens-by-lens critique

  a. Coherence — SURVIVES  
  • What it did: Noted that both “institutional economics” and “ecology” use the term “governance” to mean “mechanisms for regulating common‐pool resources.”  
  • What’s wrong:  
    – Superficial term‐matching. It never checks whether the underlying causal models in the two domains really map onto one another (e.g. resource dynamics + human incentives in irrigation systems vs. purely ecological feedbacks).  
    – Fails to probe potential equivocations in scale (small community vs. whole ecosystem) or actors (human institutions vs. biological processes).  
  • In short, the reasoning is too cursorily based on a shared buzzword, not on a genuine structural isomorphism.  

  b. Testability — SURVIVES  
  • What it did: Pointed to Ostrom’s book and her eight design principles, argued that the hypothesis is directly supported by empirical field studies and thus easily checkable.  
  • What’s right: This is precisely what a testability lens should do—identify concrete, disprovable evidence (e.g. documented case studies showing self‐organized monitoring and sanctioning).  
  • Minor quibble: It could have spelled out one or two clear “if‐then” conditions (e.g. “If a community lacks graduated sanctions and still sustains the resource, the hypothesis is falsified”) but overall the reasoning is sound.  

  c. Triviality — REFUTED  
  • What it did: Stripped away the domain‐specific language and concluded the claim is just “complex systems manage shared resources,” thus generic and uninteresting.  
  • What’s wrong:  
    – Conflates generality with triviality. The hypothesis is a nontrivial, historically novel finding precisely because it overturned a decades-dominant theory (Hardin’s tragedy).  
    – Ignores the specificity of the eight design principles, the institutional innovations (monitoring, graduated sanctions, conflict‐resolution), and the breadth of field evidence across irrigation, fisheries, forests.  
    – A proper triviality test would ask “Does this add a mechanism or prediction that was not already obvious to the target community?” Here it clearly does.  

2. Verdict & scoring

  • Final survival (2/3) is the correct outcome: a true, non-vacuous claim should not be refuted.  
  • The triviality lens miscalibration is the only blemish; it almost killed a genuine Nobel‐prize insight by applying an overly crude “generic statement = trivial” rule.  
  • Points=17 and COLLISION/SURVIVED are defensible given the pipeline’s rules—but flag that triviality should not be weighted so heavily when it so clearly misfires on landmark findings.  

3. Sharpened lens formulations

  a. Coherence (structural‐mapping lens) should require:  
    – Identification of core variables and causal pathways in each domain (e.g. resource stock, user incentives, sanctioning costs).  
    – An explicit mapping showing those variables play the same roles and satisfy the same functional relations.  
    – A check for scale or actor mismatches that would break the mapping.  

  b. Testability (falsifiability lens) should require:  
    – A clear statement of what observations or experiments would count as disconfirming evidence.  
    – Specification of key measurable indicators (e.g. resource withdrawal rates, sanction frequencies).  

  c. Triviality (novelty lens) should require:  
    – Comparison to the pre‐existing literature’s dominant paradigms.  
    – Assessment of whether the claim introduces genuinely new mechanisms or predictions.  
    – A bibliometric or citation‐analysis check: if the claim is already extensively discussed as a breakthrough, it is non-trivial by definition.

1. Lens-by-lens critique  
• Coherence (SURVIVES): Sound. The lens correctly checks that “bounded rationality” and “heuristic search” are being used in the same formal sense (pruned‐space satisficing) rather than conflating different ideas. I see no internal flaw in calling the bisociation coherent.  
• Testability (SURVIVES): Unsound. The lens treats the mere citation of a named theory (Simon’s bounded rationality) and historical facts (Logic Theorist, Nobel/Turing Awards) as “testability.” But testability requires that the claim make a clear, falsifiable prediction or yield measurable observables—e.g. “If you limit the search heuristically, solution quality degrades gracefully in proportion X under conditions Y.” Simply pointing to an established theory is not the same as offering an empirical specification.  
• Triviality (REFUTED): Also unsound. The lens argues that reducing both domains to “complex systems using limited resources to find satisfactory solutions” strips away specificity, making the claim trivial. But the whole point of this bisociation is the precise mapping of a human‐psychology model onto an AI‐algorithm design principle. That cross‐domain structural alignment is non‐trivial: it spawned a research program and a Nobel Prize. The triviality lens over‐generalizes “satisficing” until it swallows the very insight it should be judging.

2. Verdict and scoring  
Because two flawed lenses “survived” and one flawed lens “refuted,” the 2-of-3 rule still promotes the entry—but that is luck, not rigor. In fact, only the coherence lens held up under scrutiny. Testability should have been flagged “weak signal” (it never operationalized the claim), and triviality should have “survived.” If we recalibrated properly, the entry would pass 3/3, not 2/3. The 17-point award (out of a presumed 20-ish scale) under-rewards the entry’s real robustness and over‐rewards the triviality lens’s mistaken rejection.

3. Sharper lens definitions  
• Testability → Falsifiable Operationalization: Require each claim to specify at least one clear, domain-specific measurement or experiment by which the bisociation’s core mapping could be confirmed or disconfirmed.  
• Triviality → Novel Structural Insight: Instead of asking “is this just a generic truism?”, ask “does the bisociation yield a new prediction, metric, or mechanism that neither domain alone would suggest?” Only claims that add no such new structural content should be killed as trivial.  
• (Coherence is fine as is, but could explicitly demand a one-to-one mapping of key variables/operators between the two domains to raise its bar.)

1. Lens-by-lens reasoning  
   
   a. Coherence  
   • What it should check: Does the hypothesis actually hang together as a correct categorical (monad) mapping?  
   • What happened: No refutation raised, implying the lens accepted all four “isomorphisms.”  
   • Why that’s unsound:  
     – The IO-monad mapping is explicitly only “partial,” yet the claim treats it as the same abstract pattern. In real category-theoretic terms, IO in one domain isn’t the same functor (nor the same category) as IO in the other—there is no single natural transformation ν that preserves the full algebraic structure.  
     – The “strong isomorphism” claims for Maybe and State gloss over domain-specific side-conditions (e.g. gradient steps never truly “fail” in the Maybe sense, and compilation passes can have side effects beyond pure state threading).  
     – A proper coherence check would demand a sketch of the actual functor categories and the unit/multiplication laws, not just informal bullet points.  
   
   b. Testability  
   • What it should check: Can you in principle carry out an experiment or formal proof to confirm the claimed isomorphism?  
   • What happened: Silence—no objection.  
   • Why that’s unsound:  
     – The hypothesis is entirely high-level and offers no concrete protocol or criterion for “measuring” the isomorphism. You can’t point to “if we run these two pipelines, we’ll see the same categorical structure emerge.” Without that, it isn’t testable even in principle.  
   
   c. Triviality  
   • What it should check: Is this just a vacuous restatement of “many systems with state or uncertainty can be expressed as monads”?  
   • What happened: Again, no flag.  
   • Why that’s unsound:  
     – Mapping any iterative process to Maybe/State/IO/Free is literally textbook functional programming 101. Claiming it as a deep cross-domain insight without identifying a genuinely non-obvious corollary or construction is trivial.  
   
2. Verdict & scoring  
   • They awarded “ADJACENT_ACTIVE” and 50 points, treating “adjacent but not the same” as a successful verification. In fact, **nothing in the web evidence confirms the core structural isomorphism**, only tool-use overlap (ML-for-compilers). By the rubric, that should be a **refutation** (“evidence of different shape”) or at best a “narrowly_missed,” not Verified.  
   • Granting full Verified/Unrefuted status here is a clear miscalibration. The hypothesis remains **unsupported**, so it should not collect points as if confirmed.  
   
3. Sharpened lens definitions  
   • Coherence should demand an **explicit sketch of the categories** involved (objects, morphisms, unit and bind laws) and point-by-point check of functoriality and naturality. If the submitter can’t supply even a toy categorical diagram, coherence fails.  
   • Testability should require a **concrete experimental or formal protocol**: e.g. “implement a translator that maps any compiler pass to a gradient-step subroutine and show observational equivalence in at least two nontrivial benchmarks.” Absent that, testability fails.  
   • Triviality should measure novelty against a **corpus of known monadic mappings**: if the proposed mapping adds no new construction beyond the generic State or Free monad pattern, it should be auto-flagged trivial.  
   
In this case, all three lenses should have flagged the hypothesis, and the final verdict should have been a refutation or “narrowly missed,” not Verified with 50 points.

1. Lens-by-lens soundness  
   a. Coherence  
      • No explicit Coherence reasoning was recorded—“none – not refuted.”  
      • Yet on inspection the core mapping (social/psychological trust ↔ cryptographic “knowledge”) is semantically incoherent. Human trust is emergent, contextual, often opaque; zero-knowledge proofs manipulate formal statements in a deterministic protocol. The lens should have flagged that the analogy collapses once you ask “What does it mean to ‘evolve’ psychological trust as a monadic state in the same sense you evolve a cryptographic proof?”  
   b. Testability  
      • Again, “none – not refuted.”  
      • The suggested tests (“analyze case studies…”) are so high-level as to be unfalsifiable. There is no concrete dependent variable or measurable coupling between “trust variance” metrics and cryptographic throughput or security parameters. A properly calibrated Testability lens would have required (1) an operational definition of social-trust variance, (2) a clear experimental design linking that to cryptographic performance, or (3) a prediction about protocol efficiency or security that could be measured.  
   c. Triviality  
      • Also “none – not refuted.”  
      • But mapping every algebraic layer (Maybe, State, IO, Free) across unrelated domains is textbook category-theory exercise rather than novel insight. This is exactly the kind of vacuous “bisociation” that a Triviality lens should catch.  

2. Verdict & scoring  
   • Awarding 50 points and classifying this as ADJACENT_ACTIVE, Unrefuted wildly overstates the maturity and substance of the hypothesis. The Phase 2 verifier correctly noted the “zero‐trust” architecture literature but also flagged the semantic mismatch—and yet the final verdict lets it sail through.  
   • I would have given this either REFUTED (due to incoherence and untestability) or at best ADJACENT_INSUFFICIENT, with a low-single-digit score.  

3. Sharpened lens definitions  
   a. Coherence: “Does every mapped construct preserve its essential semantics under the functor, or is the mapping a superficial label swap? Require a sentence-level paraphrase test: can you swap ‘trust’ for ‘knowledge’ in each claim and preserve truth?”  
   b. Testability: “Demand at least one falsifiable prediction with a defined metric. If the hypothesis invokes constructs A and B, specify how you would measure A, measure B, and test their functional relationship.”  
   c. Triviality: “Compute a baseline of random category-theory mappings between any two monadic frameworks; if your score isn’t significantly above random chaining of Maybe→Maybe, State→State, IO→IO, Free→Free, it’s trivial.”  

— In this case, none of the three lenses actually engaged with the hypothesis’s flaws, so the “Unrefuted” tag and 50-point award are miscalibrated.
